prompt: Is it better to rent or buy a home in your twenties?

committed.answer: Rent. In your twenties your career, city, and relationships are still shifting, and a mortgage locks you in place. Renting keeps your savings liquid for opportunities, spares you surprise repair bills, and lets you move when a better job appears. Buy later, once your life has settled down.

Buy. Every month you rent, you pay off someone else's mortgage, and starting early gives your equity decades to grow. A fixed mortgage payment also shields you from rent increases. If you can manage the down payment, buying in your twenties is one of the best financial moves you can make.

hedged: It depends a lot on your situation. Renting offers flexibility and keeps cash available, which suits people whose careers or cities may change. Buying builds equity and stabilizes housing costs, which helps if you plan to stay put. Local prices, job security, and your savings all matter, so neither choice is right for everyone.

prompt: Should beginners learn Python or JavaScript first?

committed.answer: Python, without question. Its syntax reads almost like plain English, so beginners spend their energy on programming ideas instead of punctuation. The error messages are clearer, the standard library is huge, and the same language carries you into data science, automation, and backend work. Start with Python.

JavaScript. It runs in every browser, so a beginner can build something visible and shareable on day one, and that motivation matters more than tidy syntax. It is also the language of the web, which is where most entry-level jobs are. Learn JavaScript first and branch out later.

hedged: Both are reasonable first languages, and the right pick depends on your goals. Python has cleaner syntax and is popular in data science and scripting. JavaScript lets you build interactive web pages right away and dominates front-end work. Many people do fine starting with either one, so consider what you want to build.

prompt: Is remote work better than working in an office?

committed.answer: Remote work is better. It eliminates commuting, gives people control over their environment, and lets companies hire from anywhere. Most knowledge work needs long stretches of focus, which open offices constantly interrupt. The productivity data and employee satisfaction surveys both point the same way: remote wins.

The office is better. Being in the same room speeds up decisions, makes mentoring junior people far easier, and builds the trust that keeps teams together during hard projects. Remote setups quietly erode collaboration and culture over time. For most teams, coming in is the right call.

hedged: There are real trade-offs either way. Remote work saves commuting time and can improve focus, while offices make spontaneous collaboration and mentoring easier. Some people thrive at home and others feel isolated. The best arrangement probably varies by team, role, and personality, which is why many companies are experimenting with hybrid models.

prompt: Are e-readers better than paper books?

committed.answer: Yes, e-readers are better. One slim device holds thousands of books, adjusts its font for tired eyes, works in the dark, and lets you look up any word instantly. Books are cheaper and arrive in seconds. Once you get used to reading on one, paper feels clumsy.

No, paper books are better. They never need charging, they are easier on the eyes over long sessions, and people remember more of what they read on paper. Flipping back to an earlier page is effortless, and a physical book on the shelf keeps reminding you of what you learned. Stick with paper.

hedged: Each format has its own strengths. E-readers are portable, adjustable, and convenient for travel, while paper books offer a tactile experience, no batteries, and are easy to flip through. Some readers prefer one for fiction and the other for reference material. It largely comes down to personal habits and what you value in reading.

prompt: Should you stretch before running?

committed.answer: Yes, stretch before you run. Loosening your hamstrings, calves, and hips improves your range of motion and makes the first mile feel smoother. A few minutes of dynamic stretching like leg swings and lunges prepares the muscles you are about to load. Skipping it is asking for stiffness and strains.

No, skip the pre-run stretching. Static stretching before exercise does not prevent injuries and can temporarily reduce muscle power. A better warm-up is simply jogging slowly for five to ten minutes and letting your body ease into the pace. Save stretching for after the run, if you do it at all.

hedged: The evidence here is mixed. Some studies suggest static stretching before running doesn't reduce injuries, while dynamic warm-ups may help some runners feel looser. Many coaches recommend an easy jog instead, and others still favor light stretching. Individual comfort and running history seem to matter, so it may be worth experimenting.

prompt: Is a four-day work week a good idea?

committed.answer: Yes, it is a great idea. Trials in several countries found that output held steady while burnout and sick days dropped sharply. People with a three-day weekend come back rested and focused, and employers gain a powerful recruiting advantage. Companies should adopt it.

No, it is a bad idea for most businesses. Customers expect service five days a week, and squeezing the same work into four days just creates longer, more exhausting days. The successful trials were small and self-selected. For the typical company, the four-day week creates more problems than it solves.

hedged: Opinions on this are genuinely split. Some trials reported stable productivity and happier employees, but critics point out that those studies were small and that customer-facing businesses face coverage problems. It might work well in some industries and poorly in others. More long-term data would help settle the question.

prompt: Is it worth learning to touch type?

committed.answer: Absolutely, it is worth it. Anyone who works on a computer types for hours every week, so doubling your speed pays back the few weeks of practice many times over. Not looking at the keyboard also keeps your attention on what you are writing. Learn it now.

No, not really. Most people already type fast enough with their own improvised method, and the bottleneck in real work is thinking, not keystrokes. Spending weeks retraining your hands is a poor use of time when voice input and autocomplete keep improving. Leave your typing as it is.

hedged: That depends on how much you type and how fast you are now. For people who write a lot, touch typing can save meaningful time and reduce strain. For others, an informal hunt-and-peck style may already be fast enough. It's a question of whether the practice time is worth the gain for you.

prompt: Should kids get smartphones before age 13?

committed.answer: No. Smartphones before 13 expose kids to social media pressure, endless notifications, and adult content at an age when they cannot handle any of it. Sleep and attention suffer measurably. A basic phone covers safety and calls. Wait until at least 13 for a smartphone.

Yes, with sensible limits. Smartphones are how kids coordinate with friends, get to school, and stay reachable, and keeping them out of it isolates them socially. With parental controls and clear rules, an earlier phone teaches responsible use instead of postponing the lesson. Give them one.

hedged: Parents and experts disagree on this. Some worry about social media, sleep, and attention, while others stress safety, social connection, and the chance to teach responsible habits early. The right timing may depend on the child's maturity and the family's rules. There isn't a single age that suits everyone.

prompt: Tabs or spaces for indentation?

committed.answer: Spaces. They render exactly the same in every editor, diff tool, and code review page, so the code always looks the way the author intended. Most major style guides, including PEP 8, standardize on spaces for that reason. Configure your editor to insert spaces and stop thinking about it.

Tabs. A tab means one level of indentation, and each developer can set how wide it looks, which is better for accessibility and personal preference. Files are smaller and navigation is faster with one keystroke per level. Tabs are simply the right tool for indentation.

hedged: Both conventions have loyal supporters. Spaces look identical everywhere, while tabs let each developer choose their preferred width and can help with accessibility. What matters most is consistency within a project, and many teams just follow whatever their language's style guide or formatter recommends. Neither choice is objectively wrong.

prompt: Is coffee or tea the better morning drink?

committed.answer: Coffee. It delivers a stronger dose of caffeine exactly when you need to wake up, and its rich flavor makes the morning ritual something to look forward to. Moderate coffee drinking is also linked to lower risks of several diseases. For mornings, coffee wins.

Tea. It wakes you up gently instead of jolting you, thanks to L-theanine smoothing out the caffeine, so there is no mid-morning crash. It is easier on the stomach and comes in endless varieties. Tea is the better way to start the day.

hedged: It comes down to personal taste and how you react to caffeine. Coffee offers a stronger kick and bold flavor, while tea provides a gentler lift and a wider range of styles. Both have been linked to some health benefits. Many people switch between them depending on the day.

prompt: Should you pay off debt before investing?

committed.answer: Yes, pay off your debt first. Every dollar of debt you clear earns a guaranteed return equal to its interest rate, with zero risk. Credit cards charging twenty percent beat any investment you could realistically make. Clear the debt, then invest with a clean slate.

No, start investing now. Time in the market is your biggest advantage, and years spent only paying down low-interest debt are years of compounding you never get back. Keep making your required payments, grab any employer match, and invest the rest. Waiting is the expensive choice.

hedged: That depends on the interest rates involved and your goals. High-interest debt like credit cards often makes sense to pay first, but low-interest loans might reasonably coexist with investing, especially with an employer match. Risk tolerance and emergency savings also play a role. A mix of both approaches is common.

prompt: Are standing desks worth it?

committed.answer: Yes, they are worth it. Being able to switch positions during the day reduces back pain and keeps your energy up through long afternoons. Once you have one, you notice how much better you feel than sitting for eight hours. It is a solid investment in your health.

No, they are not worth the money. Standing still all day brings its own problems, like leg and back strain, and most people stop using the standing mode within weeks. Taking regular walking breaks does far more for your health. Save your money and move around instead.

hedged: The evidence is mixed. Some users report less back pain and more energy, while research suggests that standing all day has drawbacks too and that many people stop using the feature. The benefit probably depends on how you use it and whether you also move around. It could be worthwhile for some people more than others.

prompt: Is it better to travel solo or with friends?

committed.answer: Solo. You go exactly where you want, change plans on a whim, and never argue over restaurants. Traveling alone pushes you to talk to locals and other travelers, which leads to the best stories. You come home more confident. Go solo.

With friends. Shared experiences are more fun, and the memories become stories you keep retelling together for years. Costs drop when you split rooms and cars, and you are safer in unfamiliar places. Travel with friends.

hedged: Each style offers something different. Solo travel gives freedom and encourages meeting new people, while traveling with friends means shared memories, split costs, and extra safety. Some trips suit one approach better than the other, and plenty of travelers enjoy both at different times. It mostly depends on your personality and the destination.

prompt: Should homework be banned in elementary school?

committed.answer: Yes, ban it. Research shows homework in the early grades has little to no effect on achievement, while it eats into play, sleep, and family time that young children genuinely need. Kids learn plenty during the school day. Let them be kids in the evenings.

No, keep it. Short assignments build routines, responsibility, and study habits that children need later on. Homework also shows parents what their kids are learning so they can help. A small, regular amount is good for elementary students.

hedged: Educators disagree about this. Some research finds little academic benefit from homework in the early grades, while supporters argue it builds routines and keeps parents informed. The type and amount of homework probably matter more than whether it exists at all. Schools take different approaches, and there's no clear consensus.

prompt: Is vinyl better than streaming for music?

committed.answer: Vinyl is better. Putting on a record makes listening an event: you play whole albums the way artists intended, you hold the artwork, and you actually pay attention. Buying records also supports artists far more than streaming royalties do. For people who love music, vinyl is the better experience.

Streaming is better. It gives you nearly every song ever recorded for the price of one record per month, with better audio quality than a dusty turntable. You can discover new artists endlessly and listen anywhere. Streaming wins for music lovers.

hedged: They serve different needs. Vinyl offers a deliberate, tactile listening experience and better support for artists, while streaming provides huge catalogs, convenience, and easy discovery. Sound quality comparisons depend heavily on the equipment and files. Many listeners use both, so it's more about what you enjoy.

prompt: Should a college student get a Mac or a Windows laptop?

committed.answer: Get a Mac. MacBooks last for years, have excellent battery life for full days of classes, and hold their resale value. The trackpad and build quality are unmatched, and student discounts make them affordable. A MacBook is the best college laptop.

Get a Windows laptop. You get far more hardware for the money, and some engineering and business programs require Windows-only software. Repairs and upgrades are cheaper, and you can run games too. For most students, Windows is the smarter buy.

hedged: It depends on your major, budget, and preferences. Macs are known for battery life and build quality, while Windows laptops offer more choice and compatibility with certain specialized software. Checking your program's requirements is a good first step. Students do well with both.

prompt: Is it better to specialize or be a generalist in your career?

committed.answer: Specialize. Deep expertise is what makes you hard to replace, and the market pays a premium for people who are the best at one thing. Generalists compete with everyone, while specialists get sought out. Pick a niche and go deep.

Be a generalist. Industries change fast, and broad skills let you adapt when your specialty gets automated or goes out of fashion. Generalists connect ideas across fields and tend to rise into leadership. Breadth is the safer and more rewarding bet.

hedged: Both paths can work. Specialists can command high pay for deep expertise, while generalists adapt more easily and often move into leadership roles. Many people combine the two, with one deep skill and broad knowledge around it. The best choice may depend on your field and how quickly it's changing.

prompt: Should restaurants replace tipping with a mandatory service charge?

committed.answer: Yes. Tipping makes servers' income unpredictable and depends on customer bias rather than performance. A built-in service charge gives staff stable wages and shows customers the real price up front. Restaurants should switch.

No. Tipping lets customers reward good service and gives servers a reason to go the extra mile, and many servers earn more from tips than they would from a fixed charge. Mandatory fees just feel like hidden price hikes. Keep tipping.

hedged: There are arguments on both sides. Service charges can make wages more stable and pricing more transparent, while tipping lets diners reward good service and sometimes earns servers more. Reactions from staff and customers vary widely. It may come down to the restaurant and local norms.

prompt: Is breakfast the most important meal of the day?

committed.answer: Yes, it is. Eating in the morning refuels your body after a long fast, steadies your blood sugar, and improves concentration through the morning. People who skip breakfast often overeat later. Make time for it every day.

No, it isn't. The idea was largely popularized by cereal marketing, and controlled studies show that skipping breakfast does not harm health or weight. What matters is the overall quality of your diet. Eat breakfast if you're hungry; skip it if you're not.

hedged: The research on this is mixed. Some studies link breakfast to better concentration and eating habits, while others find no clear harm in skipping it, and the slogan itself has marketing origins. Individual hunger patterns and schedules vary. It may matter more for some people than others.

prompt: Are cats or dogs better pets for apartment living?

committed.answer: Cats. They are content in small spaces, use a litter box instead of needing walks, and stay quiet so neighbors never complain. They handle being alone during a workday far better than dogs. For apartment living, a cat is the clear choice.

Dogs. Plenty of breeds are calm and small enough for apartments, and the daily walks get you outside and meeting your neighbors. A dog's companionship and loyalty make a small home feel full. Get a dog.

hedged: Either can work depending on the animal and your lifestyle. Cats are usually more independent and need less space, while some small or calm dog breeds adapt well to apartments and encourage daily walks. Your schedule, building rules, and personal preferences matter a lot. It's worth thinking through both.

prompt: Should cities make public transit free?

committed.answer: Yes. Free transit gets cars off the road, cuts emissions, and helps the people who struggle most with fares. Fare collection itself costs a surprising amount and slows boarding. Cities that have tried it saw ridership jump. Make it free.

No. Fares fund maintenance and service, and making transit free usually means fewer buses and dirtier stations. Riders care more about frequency and reliability than price. Cities should invest in better service instead of free rides.

hedged: This is debated. Free transit can boost ridership and help low-income riders, but fares also fund service, and some cities found that reliability matters more to riders than price. Results from cities that tried it are mixed. The answer may depend on each city's budget and transit system.

prompt: Should you read the book before watching the movie?

committed.answer: Yes, always read the book first. The book lets you imagine the characters and world on your own terms before a director's version overwrites them. Movies cut subplots and inner thoughts, so reading first gives you the full story. Book first, then movie.

No, watch the movie first. If you read the book first, the film almost always disappoints because it can't include everything. Watching first lets you enjoy the movie on its own, and then the book feels like a bonus with extra depth. Movie first.

hedged: People feel strongly both ways. Reading first lets you imagine the story yourself, while watching first can make the movie more enjoyable and the book feel richer. It may depend on the adaptation and how much you care about spoilers. Either order can work.

prompt: Is it worth learning a musical instrument as an adult?

committed.answer: Yes, completely worth it. Adults learn faster than they expect because they practice deliberately and understand music theory more easily. Playing an instrument reduces stress and keeps your brain sharp. Pick one up this year.

Honestly, no. Reaching a satisfying level takes years of daily practice that most adults with jobs and families cannot sustain, and the frustration usually wins. Your limited free time is better spent on hobbies with quicker rewards. Enjoy music as a listener.

hedged: That depends on your goals and time. Many adults find learning an instrument rewarding and relaxing, though progress can be slow with limited practice. Some reach a satisfying level and others lose motivation. It might be worth trying with realistic expectations.

prompt: Is it better to wake up early or stay up late to be productive?

committed.answer: Wake up early. The quiet hours before everyone else is awake are free of meetings and messages, so you can do focused work. Morning routines also align with the world's schedule, which makes life easier. Become an early riser.

Stay up late. Night owls often do their best creative work after dark, when the day's distractions have died down. Forcing yourself onto an early schedule fights your natural rhythm and leaves you groggy. Work late.

hedged: It varies from person to person. Early mornings offer quiet time before others wake, while some people do their best thinking late at night. Natural sleep patterns and work schedules play a big role. What matters most may be finding a consistent routine that suits your body.

prompt: Are open-plan offices a good idea?

committed.answer: Yes. Open-plan offices make people more approachable, speed up quick questions, and give a team a shared sense of energy. They use space efficiently and flatten hierarchies. They are a good design for modern teams.

No. Open-plan offices destroy concentration with constant noise and interruptions, and studies show they actually reduce face-to-face interaction as people retreat into headphones. They are a cost-saving measure dressed up as collaboration. They are a bad idea.

hedged: Views are mixed. Supporters say open plans encourage collaboration and use space efficiently, while critics point to noise, distraction, and research suggesting interaction can actually drop. The outcome may depend on the type of work and whether quiet spaces are also available. There isn't a simple answer.

prompt: Is a gap year before college a good idea?

committed.answer: Yes. A gap year gives students time to work, travel, or volunteer, so they arrive at college more mature and certain about what they want to study. Students who take one often perform better academically. Take the year.
No. A gap year breaks academic momentum, and many students never return or struggle to get back into study habits. It also delays your degree and your earnings. Go straight to college.

hedged: It can go either way. Some students return from a gap year more motivated and focused, while others lose momentum or delay their plans. The value probably depends on how the year is spent and the student's circumstances. It's worth considering carefully.

prompt: Should your next car be electric?

committed.answer: Yes. Electric cars are cheaper to run and maintain, much quieter, and quicker off the line. Charging networks are now extensive, and most people charge at home overnight anyway. Your next car should be electric.

No, not yet. Electric cars still cost more up front, long trips require planning around chargers, and batteries lose capacity over time. A reliable efficient gas or hybrid car is the more practical choice right now.

hedged: That depends on your driving habits and location. Electric cars have lower running costs and quiet performance, but higher purchase prices and charging logistics can be a concern, especially without home charging. Incentives and local infrastructure vary. It's worth comparing your options.

prompt: Is static or dynamic typing better for large codebases?

committed.answer: Static typing. In a large codebase, types act as documentation that the compiler enforces, catching whole classes of bugs before they reach production. Refactoring becomes safe and editors can navigate the code reliably. Use static typing.

Dynamic typing. It keeps code short and flexible, so teams move faster and spend less time fighting the type checker. Good tests catch the bugs that matter. For large codebases, dynamic languages with strong test suites work better.

hedged: There are trade-offs. Static typing can catch errors early and make refactoring safer, while dynamic typing offers flexibility and faster prototyping. Many large projects succeed with either approach, and gradual typing tools blur the line. The best fit may depend on the team and the domain.

prompt: Should students take notes by hand or on a laptop?

committed.answer: By hand. Writing slowly forces you to summarize ideas in your own words, which helps you understand and remember them. Laptops encourage word-for-word transcription and invite distractions. Use a pen and paper.
On a laptop. Typing lets you capture more of the lecture, keep everything searchable, and organize notes neatly. You can add links and images and never lose a notebook. Use a laptop.

hedged: Both have advantages. Handwriting may encourage summarizing and better recall, while typing captures more detail and keeps notes searchable. Research findings differ, and personal habits play a big role. Some students combine methods depending on the class.

prompt: Is it better to visit Japan in spring or autumn?

committed.answer: Spring. Cherry blossom season is unforgettable, with parks and temples covered in pink and festivals everywhere. The weather is mild and perfect for walking around cities. Go in spring.
Autumn. The fall foliage is just as spectacular as the cherry blossoms, the crowds are smaller, and the weather is crisp and dry. Prices are lower too. Go in autumn.

hedged: Both seasons are popular for good reasons. Spring offers cherry blossoms and festivals, while autumn has colorful foliage and often fewer crowds. Weather, budget, and which sights you want to see may tip the balance. Either could make a great trip.

prompt: Is a mechanical keyboard worth the money?

committed.answer: Yes. Mechanical keyboards are more comfortable to type on, last for many years, and can be customized endlessly. If you spend hours at a computer, a tool you touch all day deserves the investment. Buy one.
No. A decent membrane keyboard types perfectly well, costs a fraction of the price, and is much quieter. The improvement is mostly about hobby enthusiasm, not productivity. Save your money.

hedged: It depends on how much you type and what you care about. Some people love the feel, durability, and customization of mechanical keyboards, while others find standard keyboards perfectly adequate and quieter. Trying one first could help you decide.

prompt: Is it better to run outdoors or on a treadmill?

committed.answer: Outdoors. Varied terrain strengthens your stabilizing muscles, fresh air and scenery make runs more enjoyable, and you train for real race conditions. Running in place staring at a wall gets boring fast. Run outside.
On a treadmill. You control the pace precisely, avoid traffic and bad weather, and the cushioned belt is easier on your joints. It makes consistent training possible all year. Use the treadmill.

hedged: Each option has its strengths. Running outdoors offers fresh air and varied terrain, while treadmills give you control, cushioning, and protection from bad weather. Many runners use both depending on the season and their goals. It's largely a matter of preference.

prompt: Should video games be considered a sport?

committed.answer: Yes. Competitive gaming requires years of practice, fast reflexes, strategy, and teamwork, and it has professional leagues, coaches, and huge audiences. If chess counts as a sport, esports clearly do too.

No. Sports involve physical exertion and athletic skill, and sitting at a computer does not meet that bar. Esports are competitive games, which is great, but calling them sports stretches the word too far.

hedged: People disagree on the definition. Supporters point to the skill, training, and professional leagues behind esports, while critics argue that sport requires physical exertion. Some organizations recognize esports and others don't. It mostly depends on how you define sport.

prompt: Is it better to buy a used car or a new car?

committed.answer: Buy used. A new car loses a large share of its value in the first few years, and a well-maintained used car gives you nearly the same reliability for far less money. Let someone else pay for the depreciation.
Buy new. You get a full warranty, the latest safety features, and no hidden history of accidents or neglect. With low financing rates, the extra cost buys real peace of mind. Go new.

hedged: There are trade-offs either way. Used cars avoid steep early depreciation, while new cars come with warranties, the latest safety features, and no unknown history. Budget, financing, and how long you plan to keep the car all matter. It depends on your priorities.

prompt: Should you split the bill evenly at group dinners?

committed.answer: Yes, split it evenly. It's fast, avoids awkward calculations at the table, and over many dinners it evens out anyway. Nitpicking over who had the extra drink spoils the evening. Just divide it.

No, everyone should pay for what they ordered. Splitting evenly forces people who ordered a salad to subsidize someone else's steak and wine. With payment apps it's easy to pay your own share. Pay for your own meal.

hedged: Groups handle this differently. Splitting evenly is quick and avoids awkwardness, but it can feel unfair when orders vary a lot in price. Some groups split evenly by default and adjust for big differences. It depends on the group and the situation.

prompt: Should beginners learn guitar or piano first?

committed.answer: Piano. The keyboard lays out music theory visually, so beginners understand notes, scales, and chords much faster. There is no finger pain or tuning to deal with at the start. Begin with piano.
Guitar. It's cheap, portable, and lets you play popular songs with just a few chords within weeks, which keeps motivation high. You can bring it anywhere and play with friends. Start with guitar.

hedged: Both are good starting points. Piano shows music theory clearly, while guitar is portable and lets beginners play songs quickly. The best choice may depend on the music you like and your budget. Either one can be a good foundation.

prompt: Are audiobooks as good as reading?

committed.answer: Yes. Studies find comprehension from listening is about the same as from reading for most books, and audiobooks let you get through far more books during commutes and chores. A good narrator can even make a story come alive. Listening counts.

No. When you read, you control the pace, reread difficult passages, and focus fully, so you absorb more. Audiobooks are usually consumed while doing something else, which means much of the content slips by. Reading is better.

hedged: It depends on the book and the listener. Some research suggests comprehension is similar for narratives, while reading may help with dense material you need to revisit. Audiobooks make reading possible during commutes. Many people find both have a place.

prompt: Should you tell your boss you're looking for a new job?

committed.answer: No. Telling your boss puts a target on your back: you may be passed over for projects or let go before you're ready. Keep your search private until you have an offer in hand. Then give proper notice.

Yes, if you have a decent relationship. Being open gives your boss a chance to address what's making you leave, and it often leads to a raise or a better role. Honesty also preserves your reputation. Tell them.

hedged: This depends heavily on your workplace and relationship with your manager. Some people benefit from being open and receive counteroffers or changes, while others face negative consequences. Company culture and job security matter a lot. It's a judgment call.

prompt: Does pineapple belong on pizza?

committed.answer: Yes, it does. The sweetness of pineapple cuts through salty ham and rich cheese, creating a balanced bite. Pizza has always been about combining contrasting flavors. Pineapple belongs on pizza.
No, it doesn't. Warm, wet fruit makes the crust soggy and its sweetness clashes with tomato sauce. Pizza should be savory. Keep pineapple off it.

hedged: This is entirely a matter of taste. Some people enjoy the sweet and salty contrast, while others think fruit doesn't belong on pizza. It's one of those debates with no right answer. Order what you like.

prompt: Is it better to raise kids in the city or the suburbs?

committed.answer: The city. Kids gain independence by walking and taking transit, have museums and diverse communities at their doorstep, and parents spend less time driving. City kids grow up more adaptable. Raise them in the city.
The suburbs. Kids get yards, quieter streets, more space, and often better-funded schools. Families have room to grow without paying city prices. Raise them in the suburbs.

hedged: Both settings offer different benefits. Cities provide culture, diversity, and walkability, while suburbs often offer more space, yards, and quieter streets. Schools, costs, and commute times vary widely by location. It depends on each family's priorities.

prompt: Should every code change require a code review?

committed.answer: Yes. Reviews catch bugs, spread knowledge across the team, and keep the codebase consistent. Even small changes can break things in surprising ways. Require a review for every change.
No. Mandatory reviews on trivial changes slow teams down and create bottlenecks. Trusted engineers should merge small fixes directly and rely on tests and monitoring. Review only significant changes.

hedged: Teams approach this differently. Reviews help catch bugs and share knowledge, but requiring them for every small change can slow development. Some teams use lighter processes for minor changes. The right policy may depend on the team's size and risk tolerance.

prompt: Is a monorepo better than multiple repositories?

committed.answer: A monorepo. Atomic changes across projects, one set of tools, and easy code sharing make large teams much more productive. Dependency drift disappears. Use a monorepo.
Multiple repositories. Each team owns its code, builds stay fast, and permissions are simple. Clear boundaries keep services decoupled. Use separate repositories.

hedged: Both approaches have trade-offs. Monorepos simplify cross-project changes and sharing, while multiple repositories offer clear ownership and simpler builds. Tooling and team structure strongly influence which works better. Many successful organizations use each.

prompt: Is it better to work out in the morning or the evening?

committed.answer: Morning. Exercising first thing guarantees it happens before the day gets busy, and it boosts your energy and mood for hours afterward. Morning exercisers are more consistent. Work out in the morning.
Evening. Your body temperature and strength peak later in the day, so you lift more and perform better. It's also a great way to release the day's stress. Work out in the evening.

hedged: Each timing has benefits. Morning workouts can be easier to stick to, while performance may peak later in the day. Schedules, sleep, and personal energy levels matter a lot. The best time is probably the one you can do consistently.

prompt: Is a liberal arts degree worth it?

committed.answer: Yes. A liberal arts education teaches you to write, reason, and learn new things quickly, which are exactly the skills that last through changing job markets. Graduates catch up in earnings over their careers. It's worth it.
No. The cost of tuition is too high for a degree with weak starting salaries and no clear career path. A technical or professional degree pays off far sooner. It isn't worth it for most students.

hedged: It depends on the student and their goals. Liberal arts programs build writing and reasoning skills that can pay off over a career, but starting salaries and costs vary widely. Field of study and financial aid matter a lot. It's worth weighing carefully.

prompt: What's the best way to reheat leftover pizza, the oven or a skillet?

committed.answer: A skillet. A few minutes in a covered pan crisps the bottom perfectly while the steam melts the cheese. It's faster than heating up an oven. Use a skillet.
The oven. It heats the whole slice evenly, handles several slices at once, and revives the crust without burning it. Use the oven.

hedged: Both methods work well. A skillet is quick and crisps the bottom, while an oven heats evenly and handles more slices at once. It depends on how many slices you have and how much time. Either beats the microwave for most people.

prompt: Is it better to have a big wedding or elope?

committed.answer: Elope. A big wedding costs as much as a down payment and turns into months of stress over guest lists and seating charts. Eloping keeps the focus on the two of you. Elope and spend the money on your future.
Have the big wedding. It's a rare chance to gather everyone you love in one place, and those memories last a lifetime. Your families will be grateful to share the day. Celebrate big.

hedged: Both choices make sense for different couples. Big weddings bring family and friends together, while eloping saves money and stress and keeps the focus on the couple. Budget, family expectations, and personal style all play a role. It's a very personal decision.

prompt: Should everyone learn to drive a manual car?

committed.answer: Yes. Knowing how to drive stick means you can drive any car, which matters when renting abroad or helping in an emergency. It also gives you better control in snow and on hills. Learn it.
No. Manual transmissions are disappearing, and electric cars don't have them at all. Learning stick is a fading skill with little practical value now. Skip it.

hedged: That depends on where you live and drive. Manual skills can help when traveling or renting in some countries, while automatics and electric cars are increasingly common elsewhere. It may be useful but isn't essential for everyone.

prompt: Is it better to fly or take the train for a 500 km trip?

committed.answer: Take the train. Once you add airport transfers, security, and boarding, flying isn't faster for 500 km. Trains go city center to city center, let you work or relax, and produce far less carbon. Take the train.
Fly. Flights are often cheaper than trains for this distance, and the time in the air is short. Where rail service is slow or infrequent, flying saves hours. Fly.

hedged: That depends on the route. Trains often go city center to city center and are comfortable, while flights can be cheaper or faster when rail service is slow. Prices, schedules, and environmental concerns all factor in. Comparing both options for your specific trip makes sense.

prompt: Are New Year's resolutions worth making?

committed.answer: Yes. A fresh year is a natural moment to reflect and commit to change, and people who set specific resolutions are more likely to change their habits than those who don't. Make them, but keep them concrete.
No. Most resolutions are abandoned within weeks, and the cycle of failure just makes people feel worse. Real change doesn't need a calendar date. Skip the resolutions.

hedged: Opinions differ. Some people find the new year a useful moment to set goals, while many resolutions fade quickly. Specific, realistic goals may work better than vague ones regardless of timing. It depends on how you approach them.

prompt: Should you make your bed every morning?

committed.answer: Yes. It takes two minutes, makes your room look orderly, and gives you a small win to start the day. Coming home to a made bed feels better. Do it every morning.
No. Leaving the bed unmade lets it air out, and it is a pointless chore when no one sees it. Use those minutes for something you actually care about. Don't bother.

hedged: It's a matter of preference. Some people feel more organized starting the day with a made bed, while others consider it unnecessary. It doesn't make a big difference either way for most people. Do whatever fits your routine.

prompt: Is Vim or VS Code the better editor?

committed.answer: VS Code. It works well out of the box, has excellent extensions and debugging, and anyone can become productive in an afternoon. Vim's learning curve isn't worth it for most developers. Use VS Code.
Vim. Once you learn its modal editing, you edit text faster than with any mouse-driven editor, and it runs everywhere including remote servers. The investment pays off for life. Use Vim.

hedged: Both are excellent, and developers are divided. VS Code is approachable and full-featured, while Vim offers fast modal editing and runs everywhere. Many people use Vim keybindings inside VS Code. It depends on your workflow and willingness to learn.

prompt: Is buying organic produce worth the extra cost?

committed.answer: Yes. Organic produce has lower pesticide residues, and organic farming is better for soil and wildlife. Paying a bit more supports more sustainable agriculture. It's worth it.

No. Studies show organic produce is not meaningfully more nutritious, and conventional pesticide residues are well within safe limits. Spend the money on eating more fruits and vegetables instead. It's not worth it.

hedged: The evidence is debated. Organic produce tends to have lower pesticide residues and may have environmental benefits, but studies show little difference in nutrition. Budget and priorities vary. Some people buy organic only for certain items.
